chapter_theme: Songs at Kanchipuram (காஞ்சீபுரம், 2 of 3), nearly all closing on Murugan as the beautiful lord of Kachi (கச்சிச் சொக்கப் பெருமாளே): in tight doubled-consonant rhythms the poet confesses bondage to women, the body of bone and skin, old age, the heirs dividing his goods and the burning of the corpse, and asks for the feet, pure devotees and the gift of Tamil; two songs are love laments for a girl sick for Murugan.
structure_note: Courtesans and women (323, 326, 328, 332, 335, 336); the body, birth and death (324 to 327, 330, 331, 333); short songs (329, 330); and two akam laments in another's voice (334, 337). Many lines are built from doubled consonants (த்த, க்க, ச்ச) for the rhythm, so word division is often uncertain.

323.reading: The poet asks not to whirl in the confusion of desire for women's coral lips and dark hair, not to wander tending this pot of bone, semen, blood, fat and skin, and not to languish in suffering, but to praise and worship the golden feet with their garland of lotus and kadamba. The praise names the vel that pierced the Krauncha and the golden mountain, the lord of the cock banner, who gave Indra his golden heavenly city, at Kachi, where Siva of the konrai and matted hair has the Goddess of chastity at his side.
323.nuance: எலுப்பு, சுக்கிலம், அத்தம், தடி, தொக்கு: the body is listed by its parts (bone, semen, blood, fat, skin) and called a pot (கடம்). The third line (சுதத்தத்தச் சதத்தத்தப் பதத்தர்க்கு ...) is too dense to divide with confidence.

324.reading: Before the kin cry 'a little for me, a little for you' over the wealth and the gold plate, call the body-hut an illusion, lay it on the logs, burn it, bury it, and the poet falls to earth to be born again, he asks for the strength to escape the arrogant, threatening, word-twisting wicked and to sing Murugan's feet. The praise names the one who embraced Valli of the millet field, the vel that struck down the mango so that the serpent's hoods and the sea trembled, the life who gives fruit to devotees free of spreading, shrinking, trembling and bewilderment, and the one who circled the world on the green peacock for the fruit, at Kachi.
324.nuance: எனக்குச் சற்று உனக்குச் சற்று: the heirs' squabble at the deathbed is quoted, and the same words return in 325 as the poet's own craving. The plea is unusual in asking to escape wicked men (துட்டர்) rather than women. கனிக்குத் திக்கனைத்துச் சுற்றிட is the circling of the world for the fruit, as in 3 and 30.

325.reading: The poet calls the body a house walled with flesh and blood and framed with bones, and himself caught in the prison of the craving that says 'a little for me, a little for you', fallen into birth, bewildered in sleep and dream and suffering the states of the soul; he asks whether he will rather wander singing the power and fame of Murugan's lotus feet. The praise names Siva of the red crescent and matted hair, who loves the green creeper at his side, the brother of the big-bellied wishing tree Ganesa, the lord of the cock banner, the vel that gives raw flesh to the drum-beating ghosts, at Kachi.
325.nuance: உறக்கச் சொப்பனத்து உற்றுத் திகைக்கப்பட்டு அவத்தைப்பட்டு: the states of sleep and dream are named as part of the soul's suffering. The last line (படுக்கைக் கச்சபத்து இச்சைப்படு கச்சி) may name the tortoise (கச்சபம) of the Kachchapesvara shrine, linked with Vishnu, but the division is uncertain.

326.reading: The poet confesses that he took the body as his own, delighted in women with fish-eyes and painted breasts, fell into their arts, cried out and grew weary in the waves of their false words; before, when he dies, they carry him to the drums, lay him on the logs, set the fire and the kin give him up and go, he asks whether he will join in devotion, hold the kadamba-adorned feet and wander singing their fame in Tamil. The praise tells of Surapadman driven into the sea and struck down, the mango pierced, and Valli of the millet field embraced, at Kachi.
326.nuance: கடத்தைப் பற்று எனப் பற்றி: the first error is clinging to the pot of the body as one's own. The funeral is told quickly (எடுத்துக் கொட்டிடக் கட்டைப்படத் ... அனல் ... கொளுத்தி), and the kin let go (பற்றற்றவர் போமுன்) before the poet does.

327.reading: The poet traces a life from the womb, growing, falling to earth and taking form, caught by things seen, until Yama counts its days, quarrels, rushes in, rages, throws the noose and seizes the breath, and the kin burn the false corpse and go home; he asks that birth and its clinging end and he be given the kadamba-adorned feet. The praise names Murugan dear to Valli of the millet field, the one who taught the Madman who burned the cities and gave his foes his golden feet, the hero who fought the mango and the boar-like demons, at Kachi where pure Tamil of the three kinds is spoken.
327.nuance: Yama's coming is given as a string of verbs (கணக்கிட்டு, பிணக்கிட்டு, கதித்திட்டு, கொதித்திட்டு, கயிற்றிட்டு, பிடித்திட்டு), counting, quarrelling, rushing, raging, noosing, seizing. பித்தனைக் கற்பித்தருள்வோனே names the teaching of Siva (the பித்தன்) without naming Om. த்ரயச் சித்ரத் தமிழ் is the threefold Tamil of verse, music and drama.

328.reading: The poet describes women who darken their teeth with betel, laugh, frown and turn their eyes, bind young men by the neck, press their breasts on them, melt them and spoil their virtue, and unite on gold-adorned beds, and asks whether, avoiding such unions, he will gain the golden feet to guard him. The praise names the vel that pierced the mango and the golden mountain, Brahma, son of the discus-bearer, fettered, and the ghosts tearing raw flesh on the battlefield, and Murugan of the kadamba garland and the fierce sakti, at Kachi.
328.nuance: சக்கரிக்குப் புத்திரற்கு உற்றுத் தளைபூண: Brahma, son of Vishnu, put in fetters, the Om story told only by its outcome. The courtesans' arts are listed but money is not named.

329.reading: A four-line song: the poet asks whether he will gain the attachment that does not suffer, seeking each day's food and clinging to wealth. The praise names the victorious vel, the one who pierced the mountain, the wisdom known by learning and experience, at Kachi.
329.nuance: தவியாத பற்று: the cure for the clinging that suffers is another clinging, to the Lord; the line can also be divided to ask for freedom from the clinging that seeks food and wealth. கற்று உற்று உணர் போதா: Murugan as the wisdom reached by learning and by experience.

330.reading: A short song: the poet, who wanders stumbling through every birth for many days, colliding and whirling, asks whether Murugan will not think to take hold of him a little. The praise names the holy feet fit to be placed on the round flower, the one who gives grace to those whose bonds are cut, at Kachi.
330.nuance: கதிதோறும் ... சுழல்வேனை: கதி here is each birth or state the soul passes through. வட்டப் புட்பத் தலம் may be the lotus of the heart where the feet are set.

331.reading: The poet asks not to worship the feet of those who give wealth, cherishing the body-hut, learning worthless words and dying and dying to be born again, but to be given Murugan's green kadamba-adorned feet to praise. The praise names the vel that struck the mango, the one sweet to Valli, the one who pierced the golden mountain, at Kachi.
331.nuance: அத்தத் தத்தத் தருவோர் தாள் அர்ச்சித்து: worshipping the feet of patrons who give gold is set against worshipping the Lord's feet, the confession of 310 in brief. செத்துச் செத்துப் பிறவாதே: repeated death and birth. The doubled syllables of the rhythm make the division of the first lines uncertain.

332.reading: The poet asks whether, not joining the pure devotees of pure mind, seeking crooked words, caught in the madness of women who bring sickness, he will be trapped in their snare, fall behind and languish. The praise names Murugan adorning Valli with the kadamba garland, sending the sakti against the mango, at Kachi of the chaste and beautiful Sakti.
332.nuance: பிணிமாதர் பெட்டிற் கட்டுத் தட்டுப்பட்டு: the women are a sickness and a box that traps. Several lines, especially the praise of the fruit given (பலம் ஈவாய்), are too dense to read confidently.

333.reading: The poet pictures himself old, hair white as a crane, its tufts falling, diseased, coughing and vomiting, learning crooked speech and stammering in many languages, carrying the false, rubbish shirt of a body-hut; he asks whether, free of that tangle, he will gain grace to speak with conviction the pure Tamil of siddhi. The praise, in drum syllables, tells of Surapadman who lost his strength, threw down his arms in fear and entered the sea as a tree, the ghosts clapping and dancing, and the sakti, at Kachi.
333.nuance: The cure for the old man's stammer (திக்கித் திக்கிக் குளறி) is pure Tamil spoken firmly (சுத்தச் சித்தித் தமிழைத் திட்டத்துக்குப் புகல). செற்றைச் சட்டைக் குடில்: the body is rubbish, a shirt and a hut at once. Sura in the sea as a tree (துருமம்) is the mango.

334.reading: Spoken for a girl sick with love for Murugan: the speaker asks that the painted creeper not be maddened and perish because of the roaring dark sea and the crescent caught by the serpent, and that Murugan give his kadamba garland. The praise names the vel that pierced the mountain and fought in the ten directions, the one sweet to the hunter girl Valli, the hero who ends the sorrow of pure devotees, at Kachi.
334.nuance: This is akam poetry in another's voice, a mother's or friend's plea for a girl, not the poet's confession. The sea's roar and the crescent are the classical torments of the lovesick; சர்ப்பத்து அத்திற் பட்டு, the moon seized by the serpent, is the eclipse. The garland asked for is the lover's token.

335.reading: The poet asks not to whirl in sorrow, tending this hollow sack of skin, a false and lying hut, learning crude and obscene speech and caught in the grief of women with hill-like breasts in golden bodices, but to join the pure devotees of pure mind and worship a little. The praise names the vel that fought the mango, Murugan who adorns Valli with the kadamba cluster, the great one, at Kachi.
335.nuance: பொக்குப் பை ... தொக்குப் பை: the body is a hollow bag of skin. The plea asks only to worship 'a little' (சற்று அர்ச்சிக்க), among the devotees. The line beginning கக்கக் கைத்தக்க is unclear.

336.reading: The poet describes women whose eyes are vel, fish and poison, breasts like mountains, hair like dark clouds, who lie with many words and melt a man's heart, so that he staggers, loses sleep and action, grieves and tires, and asks whether, not whirling so for bangled women, he will hold and worship the kadamba-adorned feet that are the golden meaning of the Vedas. The praise names the hero of the arms that embraced Valli, the pearl of the millet field, the lord of the cock banner, the one at Kachi, and the vel that destroyed the mango in the sea.
336.nuance: துயில்விட்டுச் செயல்விட்டுத் துயர்வுற்றுக் கயர்வுற்று: infatuation as sleeplessness, inaction, grief and exhaustion. சுருதிப் பொற்பொருள்: the feet are the Vedas' golden meaning. The line on Kailasa (கயிலச் சுத்த ரதத்துச் சயிலத்து) is unclear.

337.reading: Spoken for a girl sick with love: wounded by the flowers of Kama with his fish banner and by the moon that rose to fright from the poison sea, her heart is maddened and she grows weak, which is no small thing; the speaker asks Murugan to give his kadamba garland tucked with fresh jasmine. The praise names Murugan dwelling at Kachi, which green Uma desired, the vel that fights to end the faults and enemies of those who cling to him, the chest Valli embraced, and the one who cut the eight great mountains to dust.
337.nuance: Akam in another's voice, as in 334: இவள் உளம், 'her heart', is spoken by a mother or friend. Kama's arrows and the moon born with the poison of the churned sea are the torments; the cure is the god's garland.

links.note: Both speak for a girl sick with love for Murugan, wounded by Kama's flower arrows and a burning moon, and ask him to come with his garland; 337 adds that the moon rose with the poison of the sea.

Both are laments for a lovesick girl in another's voice, with the classical torments of the evening world: 24 the anril bird, south wind and crescent, 334 the roaring sea and the crescent seized by the serpent.

The Kural bids one cling to the clinging of the one without clinging in order to let clinging go; 329 asks for the clinging that does not suffer, set against the clinging to food and wealth, if its line is divided so.
Both have the heirs at the deathbed thinking of property: in 68 the young sons ask about debts and goods, in 324 the kin cry 'a little for me, a little for you' over the wealth and gold plate.
Both confess worshipping patrons for gold; 310 tells the flattery at length, 331 sets the patrons' feet (தருவோர் தாள்) against the Lord's in a few beats.

The Thiruppugazh song lists the body by its parts, எலுப்பு, சுக்கிலம், அத்தம், தடி, தொக்கு (bone, semen, blood, fat, skin), and calls it a pot (கடம்) it does not want to wander tending. The Naladiyar verse runs the same kind of list, குடரும் கொழுவும் குருதியும் என்பும் ... தோலும் ... தடியும், and asks which of these is the garlanded woman. The Naladiyar turns the catalogue on the desired woman's body, the song on the poet's own, both to undo the desire named beside it.

In 324 எனக்குச் சற்று உனக்குச் சற்று ('a little for me, a little for you') is the heirs squabbling over the dead man's gold plate. In 325 the same words name the poet's own craving (எனக்குச் சற்று உனக்குச் சற்று எனும் ஆசைச் சிறை), a prison he lives in. Read together, the heirs' greed at the deathbed is the same grasping the living man already has.

The Thiruppugazh song builds the body as a house: walls plastered with flesh and blood (இறைச்சிப் பற்று இரத்தத்து இட்டு ... சுவர் கோலி) on a frame of bone (எலுப்புக் கட்டளை). The Tirumanthiram verse also makes the body a hut, with two posts, a ridge beam and thirty-two rafters (காலும் இரண்டு முகட்டலகு ஒன்று), whose roof comes apart so the life cannot re-enter. The Tirumanthiram stresses the house's collapse, the song the prison of craving lived in while it stands.

The Thiruppugazh song tells the funeral in quick verbs: the corpse is carried, the drums beat (எடுத்துக் கொட்டிட), it is laid on the logs and the fire set (கட்டைப்பட ... அனல் ... கொளுத்தி), and the kin let go and leave. The Naladiyar verse counts the funeral drum's beats (முக்காலைக் கொட்டினுள்) until the corpse is covered and the fire taken up, the dying carrying the dead. The song uses the scene as the deadline before which it asks to sing the feet in Tamil, the Naladiyar as a call to see that the bearers are next.

The Thiruppugazh song ends a life with the kin who burn the false corpse and go home (பொய்ப் பிணத்தைச் சுட்டு அகத்திற் புக்கு அனைவோரும்). The Tirumanthiram verse has the town wail, rename him a corpse (பிணமென்று பேரிட்டு), burn him, bathe and stop thinking of him (நினைப்பொழிந்தார்களே). Both make the same point, that the kin's mourning ends at the pyre; the song then asks that the clinging of birth itself end.

The Thiruppugazh song pictures women who bind young men by the neck and unite on gold-adorned beds, and asks to avoid such unions (புணர் மாதர் பொருத்தத்தைத் தவிர்த்து) and gain the golden feet. The Naladiyar verse says those who mean to reach the right path (செந்நெறிச் சேர்தும் என்பார்) do not embrace the breasts of such women. Both make giving up that embrace the condition of reaching the goal, the Naladiyar as a rule, the song as a plea.

The short Thiruppugazh song praises the holy feet fit to be set on the round flower (வட்டப் புட்பத் தலம் மீதே வைக்கத் தக்க திருபாதா) and asks the Lord to take hold of one whirling through every birth. The Kural speaks of the great feet of the one who moved upon the flower (மலர்மிசை ஏகினான் மாணடி) and promises long life to those who reach them. The flower that bears the feet is shared; if it is the heart's lotus, as the song's nuance suggests, both place the feet there.

Two songs of the same chapter make the same plea in nearly the same words: 332 fears not joining the pure devotees of pure mind (சுத்தச் சித்தத்து ... பத்தர்க்கு) and being trapped by women who bring sickness (பிணிமாதர்), and 335 asks to join the pure devotees of pure mind (சுத்தச் சித்தத்துப் பத்திப் பத்தர்க்கு ஒத்து) instead of whirling in grief over women. A near-repeat: the company of devotees is set against the company of women in both.

The Kural says good deeds must be hurried to before the hiccup rises and stops the tongue (நாச்செற்று விக்குள் மேல் வாராமுன்). The Thiruppugazh song shows the tongue already failing in old age, coughing and stammering (திக்கித் திக்கிக் குளறி), and asks to speak pure Tamil with conviction (சுத்தச் சித்தித் தமிழைத் திட்டத்துக்குப் புகல). It applies the Kural's deadline to speech itself: what must be done before the tongue fails is to praise.

The Thiruppugazh song calls the body a hollow bag of skin (பொக்குப் பை ... தொக்குப் பை), a false hut the poet keeps tending. The Naladiyar verse calls it a skin bag (தோற்பை) in which a dancer works until he leaves, after which it does not matter what is done with it. The same skin bag serves the Naladiyar to show the body's worthlessness once the life goes, and the song to show the folly of tending it while alive.

The Thiruppugazh song describes women's eyes as vel, fish and poison (அயில் அப்புக் கயல் ... நச்சுக் கண்) and confesses that the poet staggers, loses sleep and work, and whirls for them. The Naladiyar verse names the same figures, darting carp and spears (பொருகயல் வேல்), refuses to give way to them, and sees the eye as a scooped-out palm fruit. The song is the man who gave way, the Naladiyar the one who will not.

Song 325: unflagged garble கொடிக்குக்டக் (line 427), probably கொடிக்குக் (with a stray ட்).
